name: What it became
note: Sixty INVASION events. Twenty of them supersede the document's thin lines so that the `becomes` field, which every invasion is required to carry and which every one of them was carrying as the string "nothing", finally says something. An invasion rendered purely as destruction tells a false story.

events.title: Achaemenid annexation of Gandhara and Hindush
events.evidence: The Behistun and Persepolis inscriptions listing Hindush among the satrapies, and the Aramaic documents that follow.
events.becomes: Aramaic script in daily use, and the Kharoshthi derived from it; the satrapy as an administrative model; a tribute assessment in gold that Herodotus says was the empire's largest.
events.note: Literacy returns to the subcontinent after sixteen centuries, and it arrives as somebody else's paperwork.

events.title: Alexander's campaign, and the mutiny at the Beas
events.evidence: Arrian, Curtius and Diodorus, all working from Ptolemy and Aristobulus, and the Nearchus coastal log.
events.becomes: The Indo-Greek kingdoms, bilingual coinage, the Milindapanha, and a Gandharan sculptural idiom that would put a Greek drape on a Buddha.

events.title: The Seleucid war ends in a marriage treaty and five hundred elephants
events.evidence: Strabo and Appian on the treaty, and Megasthenes' embassy that followed it.
events.becomes: An embassy at Pataliputra, the Indica, and the first sustained description of India by an outsider who lived there.

events.title: The Kalinga war
events.evidence: The thirteenth rock edict, which gives the numbers — a hundred and fifty thousand deported, a hundred thousand killed — and is the conqueror's own account.
events.becomes: The dhamma policy, the edicts, the missions to Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kings, and the only surviving instance of an ancient ruler publishing his own remorse.
events.note: The empire's greatest victory, and the reason its ruler stopped conquering.

events.title: The Indo-Greeks come down through the passes
events.evidence: The bilingual coin series in Greek and Kharoshthi, and the Yuga Purana's account of a Yavana advance to Pataliputra.
events.becomes: Menander's kingdom, the Milindapanha, the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, and a coinage tradition with a portrait on it.

events.title: The Sakas take Sindh, Gujarat and the western Deccan
events.evidence: The Saka coin series, the Mathura lion capital, and the Western Satrap inscription record.
events.becomes: The Shaka era of 78, still one of India's two calendars; the Western Satraps' dated coinage, which is the most precisely fixed sequence in ancient Indian numismatics; and the Junagadh inscription.

events.title: The Kushans arrive and stay four hundred years
events.evidence: The Rabatak inscription, the Kushan coin series, and the Gandharan and Mathuran sculptural record.
events.becomes: The workshops that made the first images of the Buddha; a coinage naming Greek, Iranian and Indian gods together; the Silk Road link that carried Buddhism to China; and Kanishka's council.
events.note: The single clearest case for the becomes field. Rendered as destruction, this is a false story.

events.title: The Alchon Hunas break through, and keep breaking through
events.evidence: The Bhitari and Junagadh inscriptions, the Alchon coin series, and Mihirakula's Gwalior inscription.
events.becomes: The Gupta fiscal collapse and, out of it, the regional kingdom as the normal political form for the next six centuries. Also the end of Taxila as a place of learning.

events.title: The Arab conquest of Sindh
events.evidence: The Chachnama, written later and from the victors' side, and the Arab geographers' descriptions of Mansura and Multan.
events.becomes: A durable scholarly and commercial link to the Abbasid world: Indian astronomy and numerals at Baghdad by 771, Al-Biruni's Sanskrit two centuries after that, and the sea trade the Gulf ports ran on.

events.title: Mahmud of Ghazni reaches Somnath
events.evidence: The Ghaznavid court histories, Al-Biruni who travelled with the campaigns, and the temple's rebuilding record.
events.becomes: Al-Biruni's Tarikh al-Hind, written because a scholar attached to the campaigns learned Sanskrit and read the sources; and, in the other direction, six centuries of argument about the raid that are still going on.

events.title: Second Tarain: the hinge of the medieval period
events.evidence: The Persian chronicles, and the abrupt change in the epigraphic and numismatic record across the north.
events.becomes: The Delhi Sultanate; Persian as a court and literary language; Amir Khusrau, who wrote in it and in Hindavi both; the Indo-Islamic building tradition; and the arrival of paper, which cut the cost of a copy by an order of magnitude.

events.title: Bakhtiyar Khalji takes Nadia and then Bengal
events.evidence: The Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, and the coin and inscription record of the new Bengal administration.
events.becomes: The Bengal Sultanate, which within a century was patronising Bengali rather than Persian — the first state anywhere to give the language a court.

events.title: Genghis Khan reaches the Indus and turns back
events.evidence: Juzjani and Juvaini, and the Sultanate's own account of Jalal ad-Din's flight across the river.
events.becomes: A frontier policy: for eighty years the Sultanate's whole military effort goes into the northwest, which is why it takes so long to move south.

events.title: Alauddin Khalji raids Devagiri and finds the Deccan open
events.evidence: Barani and Amir Khusrau, and the sudden appearance of Deccan bullion in Delhi's coinage.
events.becomes: The southern campaigns that follow, the Tughlaq capital at Daulatabad, and — indirectly — Vijayanagara, founded by men who had served in Delhi.

events.title: Timur sacks Delhi and leaves within a fortnight
events.evidence: The Zafarnama, and Timur's own memoir, which counts the dead as an achievement.
events.becomes: The Sultanate's authority breaks and the regional sultanates — Jaunpur, Malwa, Gujarat, Bengal — become independent centres of patronage in their own languages.

events.title: First Panipat: field artillery decides a battle in India
events.evidence: The Baburnama, which describes the tulughma and the carts chained together, and the Lodi coinage that stops.
events.becomes: The Mughal empire, the Ain-i-Akbari's revenue survey, a workshop tradition in painting, and the argument about sovereignty that Akbar's court conducted in public.

events.title: Talikota, and Vijayanagara is emptied
events.evidence: Ferishta and the Portuguese accounts, and the burnt layer across the city's excavated core.
events.becomes: The Deccan sultanates inherit the south, and the Nayaka successor states inherit Vijayanagara's temple and irrigation administration and run it for another two centuries.

events.title: Nadir Shah takes Delhi and the treasury with it
events.evidence: The Persian and Mughal court accounts, and the disappearance of the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor from the Indian record.
events.becomes: Mughal solvency ends. The provinces stop remitting, the Marathas, the Nizam and Awadh become the real powers, and the Company acquires an opening it did not have to fight for.

events.title: Third Panipat
events.evidence: The Maratha and Afghan accounts, and the correspondence of the Peshwa's camp before and after.
events.becomes: Maratha expansion north stops. Neither victor holds Delhi. The vacuum is filled four years later at Buxar, by a trading company.

events.title: Plassey, and then the Diwani
events.evidence: The Company's own correspondence, the treaty with Mir Jafar, and the 1765 grant of the diwani of Bengal.
events.becomes: A trading company acquires the revenue of a province and stops having to ship bullion to buy Indian goods. The Drain opens, and it is an accounting fact before it is a policy.

events.title: Ajatashatru breaks the Vajji confederacy with siege engines and diplomacy
events.evidence: The Pali accounts of the mahashilakantaka and the rathamusala, and of the minister sent to divide the assembly first.
events.becomes: The republican form loses its strongest example. Magadha's method — split the assembly, then besiege — becomes the template for absorbing a gana-sangha.

events.title: Kharavela of Kalinga campaigns north and brings back a Jain image
events.evidence: The Hathigumpha inscription, which is his own account and dates itself by regnal year.
events.becomes: Kalinga's brief reassertion, and the retrieval of an image taken by the Nandas three centuries earlier — an early instance of restitution as a war aim.

events.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni destroys the Kshaharatas
events.evidence: The Nasik inscription of his mother Gautami Balashri, and the restruck Nahapana coins found at Jogalthembi.
events.becomes: Satavahana revival and the Deccan trade routes reopened; the restruck coins are the clearest physical record of a conquest in ancient India.
events.note: He melted down the enemy's coins and struck his own over them. Twelve thousand of them were found in one pot.

events.title: Samudragupta campaigns to Kanchi and restores every king he defeats
events.evidence: The Allahabad pillar inscription, which names twelve southern kings and says they were captured and released.
events.becomes: The mandala made explicit: a defeated king restored is a tributary, and a tributary is worth more than a province. The doctrine outlives the dynasty by a thousand years.

events.title: Pulakeshin II halts Harsha at the Narmada
events.evidence: The Aihole inscription of Ravikirti, and Xuanzang's independent account of both courts.
events.becomes: The Narmada stays a political boundary. The north never again forms a single state that reaches the Deccan until the Mughals.

events.title: The Pallavas sack Vatapi in reply
events.evidence: Narasimhavarman's Badami inscription, cut on the rock of the captured capital.
events.becomes: A century and a half of Pallava-Chalukya exchange in which each side copies the other's architecture. Pattadakal's northern and southern towers stand side by side because of it.

events.title: The Rashtrakutas sack Kannauj and go home
events.evidence: The Rashtrakuta grant record, and Al-Masudi's report that the Balhara was the greatest king of India.
events.becomes: The Deccan becomes the arbiter of the north without ever trying to hold it — and spends the proceeds on Ellora.

events.title: Rajaraja takes Anuradhapura and moves the capital
events.evidence: The Chola inscriptions in Sri Lanka, the Mahavamsa's account, and the Shiva temples built at Polonnaruwa.
events.becomes: Polonnaruwa becomes the island's capital and stays so for three centuries after the Cholas leave; and a Tamil-speaking population is established in the north that is still there.

events.title: The Chola fleet crosses the Bay and raids Srivijaya
events.evidence: The Tanjore inscription listing the ports taken, and the Chinese record of the embassies before and after.
events.becomes: The Bay of Bengal trade reorganises around Chola-protected routes; the Ayyavole guild operates from Java to the Gulf; and an embassy of seventy-two merchants reaches the Song court in 1077.
events.note: The only recorded transoceanic invasion launched from India. It was a trade dispute.

events.title: The Chola-Chalukya wars grind over Vengi for a century
events.evidence: Both dynasties' inscription series, which claim the same victories.
events.becomes: Exhaustion on both sides, and a Chalukya prince on the Chola throne in 1070 — the war ends in a succession, not a conquest.

events.title: The Hoysalas and Yadavas fight over the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab
events.evidence: The inscription record of both dynasties across the contested districts.
events.becomes: Both are still fighting each other when Delhi arrives, and neither can answer it.

events.title: Warangal falls to the Tughlaqs
events.evidence: The Delhi court histories, and the abrupt end of the Kakatiya inscription series.
events.becomes: The Kakatiya nayaka officers scatter south and become the Nayaka lineages of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee — the administrative class survives the state by four hundred years.

events.title: The Madurai Sultanate holds the far south for forty years
events.evidence: Ibn Battuta, who was there and married into the ruling family, and the sultanate's coinage.
events.becomes: Vijayanagara's southern expansion is organised to remove it, and the Nayaka system of military governorship is built to hold what is taken.

events.title: The Bahmani secession divides the Deccan for two centuries
events.evidence: The Bahmani coinage and court chronicles, and the Tughlaq record of the revolt.
events.becomes: Five successor sultanates, a Persianate court culture at Bijapur and Golconda, and Dakhni — a literary language before Urdu had a name.

events.title: The Ahoms defeat seventeen Mughal invasions and record every one
events.evidence: The buranjis, which are state chronicles kept as an administrative duty, and the Mughal accounts that agree about the outcomes.
events.becomes: Assam is never annexed. The paik labour system that raised the armies survives, and so does the chronicle tradition — history as state practice, which no other Indian polity institutionalised.

events.title: Lachit Barphukan wins Saraighat on the river
events.evidence: The buranjis and the Mughal accounts of the fleet action at the Brahmaputra narrows.
events.becomes: The Mughal frontier stops at the Manas. Assam stays outside the empire until the Company arrives a century and a half later.

events.title: Shivaji sacks Surat and shows the empire is porous
events.evidence: The English and Dutch factory records, which describe the raid from inside the city.
events.becomes: A revenue system built on chauth and sardeshmukhi — a claim on somebody else's tax rather than a conquest of their land, which is far cheaper to enforce and much harder to remove.

events.title: Aurangzeb spends twenty-six years in the Deccan
events.evidence: The Mughal court histories, the campaign correspondence, and the collapse of the jagir assignment system it produced.
events.becomes: The Deccan is annexed and the empire is bankrupted doing it. The Marathas the campaign was meant to destroy hold the initiative within a decade of its end.

events.title: The Carnatic wars are fought by Indian armies under European officers
events.evidence: The Company and Compagnie records, and the subsidiary treaties with the Nizam and the Nawab of Arcot.
events.becomes: The sepoy army and the subsidiary alliance: a ruler pays for troops he does not command, and loses his revenue and then his state to the arrangement.

events.title: Buxar settles what Plassey only started
events.evidence: The battle accounts, and the Treaty of Allahabad that followed a year later.
events.becomes: The Mughal emperor grants the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to a company. Sovereignty and revenue separate, and the Company holds the half that pays.

events.title: The Mysore wars: four of them, and the last one ends the state
events.evidence: The Company records, the Mysore court correspondence, and the rocket artillery the British took back to Woolwich.
events.becomes: Congreve rockets, developed at Woolwich from Mysorean examples; and, in India, the annexation model that the Company then applied everywhere.

events.title: The Anglo-Maratha wars end the last power that could have won
events.evidence: The Company and Peshwa records, and the treaties of Salbai, Bassein and Poona.
events.becomes: Paramountcy: after 1818 no Indian state can make war or foreign policy, and the map stops being a map of states and becomes a map of dependencies.

events.title: The Anglo-Sikh wars take the Punjab, the last independent state
events.evidence: The campaign records, the Treaty of Lahore, and the annexation proclamation of 1849.
events.becomes: The subcontinent is under one authority for the first time since Aurangzeb. Eight years later it rebels.

events.title: The Rebellion, and the Crown takes over from the Company
events.evidence: The military and civil records of both sides, the trial of Bahadur Shah, and the Government of India Act 1858.
events.becomes: Direct Crown rule, the end of annexation by doctrine of lapse, a permanent garrison ratio, and a colonial state that from then on governs by census, survey and category.

events.title: The Burmese wars and the annexation of Assam and Arakan
events.evidence: The Treaty of Yandabo, and the Company's revenue settlement of Assam that followed it.
events.becomes: Assam's tea plantations, the indentured labour brought in to work them, and a demographic change that is still politically live.

events.title: The Portuguese take Goa and hold it for four and a half centuries
events.evidence: The Portuguese chancery records, and the Goa Inquisition's own archive.
events.becomes: The cartaz pass system, which made the Indian Ocean a licensed sea for the first time; the Konkani printing press; and an Inquisition that burned Konkani and Marathi manuscripts as well as people.

events.title: Cabral bombards Calicut and the licensed sea begins
events.evidence: The Portuguese accounts, and the Zamorin's alliance with the Egyptian and Gujarati fleets that followed.
events.becomes: Diu in 1509, and after it three centuries in which Indian shipping sails at somebody else's permission.

events.title: The Ghurids are beaten at Kasahrada before they win at Tarain
events.evidence: The Jain chronicles of Gujarat and the Persian accounts, which both record the defeat.
events.becomes: Muhammad of Ghor turns north instead, and the Punjab route becomes the one that matters. Gujarat buys itself another century and a half.
events.note: A defeat that redirected an invasion. The gate has more than one door.

events.title: The Sultanate turns back six Mongol invasions in twenty years
events.evidence: Barani's account of the campaigns and of Alauddin's standing army and price controls.
events.becomes: A permanent paid army, the market regulations that fed it, and a fiscal apparatus reaching into village grain prices — built to fight Mongols and then used to conquer the Deccan.

events.title: Arakanese and Portuguese raiders depopulate the Bengal delta
events.evidence: The Mughal and Portuguese accounts of the Sandwip and Chittagong raids, and the Bengali literature that records them.
events.becomes: The Mughal conquest of Chittagong in 1666, and a frontier of forest clearance and settlement that reshaped eastern Bengal.

events.title: The Kalabhras take the Tamil country, and the record goes quiet
events.evidence: Almost nothing: a few later hostile references, and a three-century gap in the inscription series.
events.becomes: Jain and Buddhist institutions flourish in the gap; and the Pallava and Pandya revivals that end it define themselves against it.
events.note: Called a dark age by people who came after and disliked them. The darkness may be ours.
